description: Primary and secondary data, qualitative and quantitative methods, interviews and observation.
content_html:
Types of Data: Primary, Secondary, Quantitative and Qualitative

Before choosing a research method, sociologists must decide what kind of data they need. Primary data is original data collected directly by the researcher — through questionnaires, interviews or observation. Secondary data is data already gathered by someone else that the researcher re-uses — government statistics, newspaper archives, historical records, diaries and journals, or published research.

Quantitative data takes numerical form — percentages, rates, frequencies, scores. It allows comparisons across large samples and can be analysed statistically. Positivist sociologists, who argue sociology should follow the methods of natural science, prefer quantitative data because it is objective and replicable. Qualitative data takes verbal form — the words, accounts, feelings and interpretations of participants. It provides depth and texture. Interpretivist sociologists, associated with interactionism, prefer qualitative data, arguing that understanding social behaviour requires grasping the subjective meanings of the participants.

Secondary sources include official statistics (produced by the Office for National Statistics, the Home Office, and other government bodies) and non-official statistics (produced by pressure groups, charities or academic bodies). Official statistics have strengths: they are large-scale, nationally consistent, free to access, and allow trends to be tracked over time. However, sociologists must evaluate them critically: crime statistics, for example, only count crimes that are reported to and recorded by the police, so the true level of offending is almost certainly higher than official figures suggest. Personal documents such as diaries and letters can also serve as qualitative secondary sources, providing insight into private experience that no survey could access.

Key Fact

The choice between quantitative (numbers, patterns) and qualitative (words, meanings) data reflects both practical constraints (scale, cost) and the researcher’s theoretical approach. Positivists prefer quantitative; interpretivists prefer qualitative. Many sociologists combine both through a mixed methods approach.

Questionnaires

A questionnaire is a standardised set of written questions distributed to a sample. Closed questions offer a fixed set of responses (e.g. yes/no, tick all that apply, a rating scale) and produce quantitative data. Open questions allow respondents to answer in their own words, producing qualitative data.

Strengths: questionnaires can reach large samples quickly and cheaply. They are standardised — all respondents answer the same questions — which improves reliability. Anonymity may encourage honest answers on sensitive topics. Weaknesses: response rates can be low, introducing bias. Closed questions impose the researcher’s categories on complex experiences. Questionnaires cannot probe or follow up unexpected answers, which reduces validity.

Interviews: Structured, Unstructured and Semi-Structured

A structured interview follows a fixed schedule of questions in the same order and wording for every participant, much like a spoken questionnaire. This produces quantitative data that is easy to compare. The weakness is limited depth — no follow-up is possible.

An unstructured interview begins with an opening topic and allows the conversation to develop naturally. It can reveal unexpected themes and rich qualitative data. The weakness is that it is time-consuming and harder to compare across participants. The interviewer effect — respondents giving socially desirable answers because of the interviewer’s characteristics — is a risk in all interview types. A semi-structured interview uses a list of key themes but allows probing; it combines comparability with depth.

A sociologist wants to investigate the experiences of young people who have left the care system. A structured interview would be inappropriate: the fixed questions might miss what matters most to participants, and the formal tone could feel clinical when discussing sensitive personal history. An unstructured interview would allow participants to lead the conversation and build the rapport needed to discuss difficult experiences honestly. The weakness is that the data would be harder to compare systematically. A semi-structured interview might offer a compromise: key themes (housing, employment, relationships) guide the conversation, but the interviewer follows up where the participant goes.

Observation: Participant and Non-Participant

Observation involves directly watching people in their natural social setting. Non-participant observation means the researcher watches without taking part. The presence of an observer may alter participants’ behaviour (the Hawthorne effect).

Participant observation means the researcher joins the group and participates in their daily life, either overtly (with the group’s knowledge) or covertly (without it). Willis’s 1977 study Learning to Labour is a classic example: Willis spent time with twelve working-class boys in their school and community, observing how they actively resisted school culture and produced their own counter-school subculture. This gave qualitative depth that no survey could produce. Participant observation is high in validity — it captures real behaviour in natural settings. Its weaknesses are that it is time-consuming, the researcher may go native (over-identify with the group and lose objectivity), and covert observation raises serious ethical concerns about deception.

Mixed Methods and Triangulation

Rather than choosing a single method, many sociologists use a mixed methods approach. For example, a study of attainment gaps might begin with a large-scale questionnaire to identify patterns, then follow up with in-depth interviews to explore the meanings behind those patterns. This strategy is sometimes called triangulation — using multiple methods so that the weaknesses of one approach are compensated for by the strengths of another.

A critical mistake on methods questions is listing generic strengths and weaknesses without applying them to the specific research context. “Observation is time-consuming” earns limited credit. “Participant observation would be particularly problematic for a study of gang violence because gaining covert access to a criminal network would put the researcher at significant personal risk and require sustained deception, raising serious ethical concerns about informed consent” earns full marks. Every evaluation point must be anchored to the specific research topic in the question.

Key Fact

Reliability (can the study be replicated with the same results?) and validity (does the study reflect real behaviour?) are the two key evaluative concepts for research methods. Questionnaires tend to score well on reliability; participant observation tends to score well on validity. Most methods trade one off against the other.
exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark Evaluate on research methods, structure your argument around three dimensions: practical (is it affordable and accessible?), ethical (does it protect participants?), and theoretical (does the method align with what the researcher wants to know — patterns vs meanings?). A Mastering-tier answer will use all three dimensions and anchor every point to the specific research context in the question. Avoid listing “pros and cons” symmetrically without making a judgement: the question asks you to evaluate, so you must weigh the evidence and reach a supported conclusion about how far the method is or is not appropriate for the specific research topic.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Primary data is collected by the researcher (questionnaires, interviews, observation); secondary data is collected by others (official statistics, diaries, published research). Quantitative data is numerical (reliability, comparison); qualitative data is verbal (depth, meaning).
  • Questionnaires are quick and reliable but may lack validity. Structured interviews are comparable; unstructured interviews produce richer data but risk the interviewer effect. Participant observation (e.g. Willis, 1977) is high in validity but raises ethical concerns around deception and going native.
  • Mixed methods and triangulation combine approaches to exploit complementary strengths. All methods evaluation must be applied to the specific research context, not stated as generic lists.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of data is expressed in numerical form and can be analysed statistically?
A) Qualitative data
B) Secondary data
C) Quantitative data
D) Primary data
Define the term 'triangulation' as used in sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating it involves using more than one method or data source; 1 mark for indicating the purpose is to cross-check findings and compensate for the weaknesses of individual methods, increasing confidence in the conclusions. Example: 'Triangulation involves using two or more research methods or data sources in the same study so that the weaknesses of one approach are compensated for by the strengths of another.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one advantage of using unstructured interviews and describe why this makes them suitable for studying sensitive social topics.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an advantage of unstructured interviews (e.g. generates rich qualitative data, allows participants to raise unexpected themes, builds rapport, follows the participant's own framework of meaning). Up to 2 marks for a developed description. Example: identifying that unstructured interviews build rapport (1 mark) and explaining that for sensitive topics such as domestic abuse or experiences of discrimination, the conversational and non-directive format allows participants to feel more comfortable sharing personal experiences; the interviewer can adjust tone and pacing in response to emotional cues, producing more honest and valid data than a standardised questionnaire (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe the strengths and weaknesses of questionnaires as a method of sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for strengths: questionnaires can reach a large sample quickly and at low cost; responses are standardised so data can be compared statistically; anonymity may increase honest responses on sensitive topics; the study can be replicated, improving reliability. Up to 2 marks for weaknesses: response rates may be low and non-respondents may differ from respondents, introducing bias; closed questions impose the researcher's categories on complex experiences; questionnaires cannot probe unexpected answers; respondents from different social groups may interpret the same question differently, reducing validity.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that official statistics are a more valuable source of data for sociologists than qualitative methods.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments supporting official statistics: large-scale, nationally consistent, free to access, allow long-term trend analysis; the Crime Survey for England and Wales provides data on millions of households. Arguments against: official statistics are limited by under-reporting (the dark figure of unrecorded crime); they are politically produced and may reflect government priorities rather than social reality; different perspectives interpret the same statistics differently (functionalist, Marxist and interactionist readings diverge). Qualitative methods (participant observation, unstructured interviews) may offer insight statistics obscure. The answer names at least two perspectives or contexts, uses sociological vocabulary (validity, reliability, dark figure), and reaches a supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides addressed; at least one named perspective or method cited; a judgement reached.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some concepts named; conclusion present but assertive.

Emerging: Basic description of statistics or methods; little evaluation; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that participant observation is the most valuable method available to sociologists studying social groups.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments in favour: participant observation produces highly valid data that captures real behaviour in natural settings; Willis (1977, Learning to Labour) reveals depth of counter-school culture not accessible by questionnaire; interactionists value it for accessing the subjective meanings of participants. Arguments against: raises serious ethical concerns (covert observation violates informed consent; participant safety may be compromised in dangerous settings); researcher may 'go native'; extremely time-consuming; findings are not generalisable beyond the specific group; positivist researchers argue it lacks reliability because it cannot be replicated. The answer evaluates practical, ethical and theoretical dimensions, cites at least two named perspectives or studies, and reaches a clear supported judgement about when and for whom participant observation is most valuable.

Secure: Arguments for and against addressed; at least one named study or perspective; a judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly one-sided or descriptive; some evaluation but undeveloped; conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic description of participant observation; little evaluation; no clear judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which research method involves the researcher directly watching behaviour without taking part in the group being studied?
Which concept refers to the risk that respondents give socially desirable answers because of the interviewer's presence or characteristics?
Willis's 1977 study '______ to Labour' used participant observation to study twelve working-class boys' counter-school culture.
Using two or more research methods to cross-check findings and compensate for individual weaknesses is called '______'.
Match each method or concept to its key strength or feature.
right: Can reach a large sample quickly and allows statistical comparison (high reliability)
Generates rich qualitative data and allows the researcher to probe unexpected answers (high validity)
Produces highly valid data by observing real behaviour in natural settings
Large-scale, free to access, and allows long-term trend analysis across the population

flashcard_questions.a: Data collected first-hand by the researcher for their specific study, e.g. through questionnaires or interviews.
Data already collected by others for different purposes, such as government statistics or published research.
A question with fixed response options that produces quantitative data.
A question allowing respondents to answer in their own words, producing qualitative data.
When respondents give socially desirable answers because of the interviewer's presence or characteristics.
A method in which the researcher joins a group and participates in their daily life to observe behaviour naturally.
Learning to Labour, 1977, participant observation with twelve working-class boys ('the lads').
When people change their behaviour because they know they are being observed or studied.

flashcard_questions.q: What is reliability in sociological research?
flashcard_questions.a: The extent to which a study can be replicated and produce consistent results.

flashcard_questions.q: What is validity in sociological research?
flashcard_questions.a: The extent to which a method measures what it claims to and reflects real, naturally occurring behaviour.
Using two or more research methods or sources to cross-check findings and improve confidence in conclusions.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do positivist sociologists value standardised methods?
flashcard_questions.a: Because standardised research instruments ask identical questions of all participants, enabling fair comparison of results.

flashcard_questions.q: What does replicability mean and why do positivists value it?
flashcard_questions.a: Replicability means the study can be repeated and should produce the same results, confirming reliability.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do positivist sociologists favour quantitative data?
flashcard_questions.a: It allows statistical comparison across large samples, identifying patterns that can be generalised to wider populations.

glossary_terms.definition: Data collected first-hand by the researcher specifically for the current study, such as through questionnaires, interviews or observations.
Data already collected by others for different purposes, such as government statistics, documents or published studies, which the researcher re-uses.
A standardised set of written questions given to respondents, producing quantitative data (closed questions) or qualitative data (open questions).
A conversational interview with no fixed questions, allowing participants to lead the discussion and producing rich qualitative data.
A research method in which the sociologist joins a group and participates in their daily life to observe behaviour in its natural setting.
Using two or more research methods or data sources to cross-check findings and compensate for the weaknesses of individual methods.
The extent to which a study can be replicated and produce consistent results across different researchers or occasions.
The extent to which a research method measures what it claims to and reflects real, naturally occurring behaviour.

hero_image_caption: Choosing the right research method depends on the question, the population being studied, and practical and ethical constraints.
